To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) AS for men with low-risk prostate cancer is a safe and feasible option, (2) AS is not associated with a higher risk of metastatic disease, (3) AS is associated with an increase in prostate cancer–specific mortality (PCSM) of 1.5% per 10-yr interval, but this risk is comparable to the risk of active treatment, and (4) the risk of PCSM is not increased in patients who are treated with radical prostatectomy

the 2-y progression-free survival (PFS) was 93.6%, the median PSA doubling time was 5.3 yr, and that 7.5% of the patients were reclassified to a higher risk category and recommended for active treatment.

(1) PSA velocity (PSAV) is not an independent predictor of prostate cancer progression, (2) the PSA density (PSAD) is not a predictor of progression, and (3) the PSAV and PSAD are not independent of each other.

AS is not yet ready to be offered as a standard of care.
we need more data from the PRIAS study and similar protocols to answer many questions about AS.
the data from the PRIAS study provide a good basis for the decision to initiate AS, but the long-term results are still pending.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the PRIAS study provides a standardised protocol for AS, and we are now able to follow patients in a uniform fashion worldwide.
we are still learning about AS, and the PRIAS study will help us learn faster.
we have a lot to learn about AS and that we should learn it from large patient cohorts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk of progression to higher-risk disease is low, even in the first year after diagnosis.
the risk of progression to higher-grade disease is very low in patients who have a PSA density (PSAd) ≤0.15 ng/ml/cm3, a PSA ≤10 ng/ml, and a biopsy Gleason score ≤6.
AS is an acceptable treatment option for patients with low-risk disease.
